strengths: Novel application of prompt injection vulnerability for LLM provenance detection with clear motivation and intuitive connection
Comprehensive large-scale experimental evaluation on 5 base models with ~700 suspect models, achieving >90% TPR (gray-box) and >81% TPR (black-box) with near-zero FPR
Addresses practically important gray-box setting (token probability access) that was previously unexplored in LLM provenance literature
Sound technical approach with well-motivated loss functions (uniqueness + robustness), principled statistical threshold calibration, and extensive ablation studies

Strong robustness analysis including evaluation under prompt-injection detectors, adaptive attacks, scaling to larger models (14B), and insightful failure analysis showing misdetections correlate with model degradation
Practical consideration of real API constraints (e.g., top-k probabilities like ChatGPT), handling of both post-training and quantization post-processing
Well-written paper with clear presentation, comprehensive appendix with algorithmic details, and reproducible methodology
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies existing GCG algorithm without modifications and combines standard loss components; primary contribution is problem application rather than methodological innovation

Fundamental dependency on prompt injection vulnerability persisting in future models; limited discussion of degradation pathway as defenses improve, and vulnerability strength may vary significantly across architectures

Significant practical deployment barriers: fingerprint construction costs 60 GPU-hours; black-box verification requires ~30,000 queries (28 minutes); real-world APIs often have strict rate limits and query budgets

Threshold calibration depends on only 13 validation models with limited sensitivity analysis; empirical threshold selection presents as statistical guarantee but lacks formal rigor; unclear robustness to validation set selection or leakage

Limited generalization analysis: only recent open-source English models evaluated; no evaluation on older, closed-source, multilingual, very small, or domain-specific models; only first token considered
Complete evasion possible under white-box attack (Table 14, TPR=0) with potential gray-box evasion (83.3%); risk management strategy for fingerprint compromise inadequately addressed

Hyperparameter choices appear somewhat arbitrary despite ablations; semantic category-based token pairing not compared against alternatives; limited principled guidance for practitioners on new models
Limited analysis of why optimization beats heuristics; IPGuard comparison somewhat unfair due to adaptation from classifiers; LLMPrint-CA failure not thoroughly explained

Scope limitations: only first-token generation used without rigorous justification; unclear if multi-token sequences could provide stronger fingerprints; intra-family generalization (e.g., different Llama sizes) not explored
Missing code URL and incomplete reproducibility details; token pair independence and correlation properties not analyzed; theoretical lower bounds on robustness not discussed

strengths: Clever and creative core idea of exploiting prompt injection vulnerabilities for fingerprinting via decision boundary alignment
Strong empirical results with high TPR (>90% gray-box, >81% black-box) and near-zero FPR across five diverse base models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation covering ~700 suspect models with extensive ablations, adaptive attacks, and detector evasion analysis
Practical contribution addressing understudied gray-box setting where models expose per-token probabilities
Sound methodology with principled statistical threshold calibration using validation models and z-scores
Honest failure analysis correlating detection failures with large benchmark performance degradation
Reproducibility emphasis with detailed hyperparameters, algorithms, and promised public code
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily applies existing GCG algorithm to a new application without methodological innovation or theoretical advancement
Robustness claims lack rigorous theoretical justification; decision boundary stability argument is intuitive but unproven for quantization and post-training
Complete vulnerability to white-box attacks (0% TPR, Table 14) represents a fundamental limitation since fingerprint prompts will be publicly available
Gray-box practicality overstated—most production APIs (GPT-4, Claude) don't expose per-token probabilities; top-k access causes 4-5% TPR drop on quantization

Evaluation methodology concerns: positive/negative definition uses models derived from different bases (not truly unrelated), no statistical significance testing, only 13 validation models for threshold calibration, and suspicious perfect zero FPR on multiple base models
Ad-hoc design choices lacking principled justification: 20 manually curated semantic categories, fixed base prompt, specific loss function forms (Eqs. 1-3), and z=1.64 threshold choice
Post-processing robustness underexplored—only quantization and post-training tested; model merging achieves only 91.4% TPR suggesting fragility under partial modifications
Limited scope of evaluation: only open-source decoder-only LLMs tested; no cross-architecture detection, no encoder-decoder or multimodal models
Circular failure analysis: failures correlate with benchmark degradation, but this doesn't validate robustness—it shows the method fails when models diverge significantly from base
Missing comparisons with many recent methods listed in Table 1; LLMPrint-CA baseline performs terribly suggesting unfair comparison setup

strengths: Novel repurposing of prompt injection vulnerability for defensive fingerprinting with intuitive decision boundary-based formulation
Highly practical focus on passive methods for already-released models, addressing real gap in prior proactive approaches
Comprehensive large-scale evaluation on 5 diverse base models and ~700 suspect models (463 post-trained, 230 quantized variants) across both gray-box and black-box settings
Strong empirical results substantially outperforming baselines: gray-box TPR >90% with FPR≈0; black-box TPR >81% with FPR<1.5% vs TRAP/LLMmap with 50-56% FPR

Thorough experimental rigor with extensive ablations on design choices, robustness evaluation under prompt injection detectors, adaptive attack analysis, and failure case analysis correlating misdetections with model degradation
Principled statistical framework for verification using Gaussian calibration on validation negatives with z-score thresholding
Exploration of previously unexplored gray-box setting (per-token probability access) reflecting practical API designs
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem, intuitive figures, and comprehensive supplementary materials enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: White-box attacks completely break method (0% TPR, Table 14) via LoRA fine-tuning to invert fingerprint, severely limiting applicability in scenarios with model access; gray-box attacks also significantly degrade performance (16.7% TPR), suggesting fingerprints have exploitable structure

Robustness claim to post-processing lacks formal theoretical justification—why should prompts near decision boundaries remain near those boundaries after post-training alters weight distributions? Robustness loss (Eq. 2) is heuristic using log-sum-exp approximation without optimality proof

Limited theoretical foundation: no formal analysis proving fingerprints unique to base models; Gaussian assumption for verification empirically validated but theoretically unjustified; z-score choice (1.64) appears arbitrary

Limited scope of evaluation restricted to open-source models; generalization to proprietary models (GPT-4, Claude) completely unclear; only 2 models tested beyond 8B parameters; only GGUF quantization format evaluated; differential performance across post-training procedures unexplored

Significant computational costs may hinder deployment: fingerprint construction requires ~60 GPU-hours; black-box verification requires 28+ minutes (300 prompts × 100 queries), potentially exceeding API rate limits

Failure analysis is somewhat circular: correlation between misdetections and model degradation shown (Table 8) but doesn't explain which post-processing operations break fingerprints without degrading general performance

Validation set composition not ablated; unclear sensitivity of threshold calibration to validation model choice; in practice, selecting appropriate validation negatives for new base models could be non-trivial

Baseline comparisons potentially incomplete: IPGuard and LLMPrint-CA perform extremely poorly (0% TPR); TRAP and LLMmap may not be optimally tuned; most related work marked unreproducible due to missing details
